reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: A rare cause of upper gastrointestinal bleeding in which blood reaches the duodenum through the pancreatic duct via the ampulla of Vater
Most often results from rupture of a splenic artery pseudoaneurysm into the pancreatic duct, usually in the context of chronic pancreatitis or a pancreatic pseudocyst
Bleeding is characteristically intermittent, producing episodic melaena or haematemesis that can be difficult to localise
Epigastric pain radiating to the back may accompany or precede bleeding as blood and clot distend the duct
A raised serum amylase together with obscure bleeding should prompt consideration of the diagnosis
Contrast-enhanced computed tomography and visceral angiography identify the culprit pseudoaneurysm
Transcatheter arterial embolisation is the preferred first-line treatment, with surgery (such as distal pancreatectomy) reserved for embolisation failure
reference.pathophysiology: Haemosuccus pancreaticus occurs when a peripancreatic artery, most commonly the splenic artery, develops a pseudoaneurysm as a result of enzymatic erosion by activated pancreatic secretions, typically in chronic pancreatitis or adjacent to a pseudocyst. Rupture of the pseudoaneurysm into the pancreatic duct allows blood to track along the duct and empty through the ampulla into the duodenum. Because the bleeding decompresses intermittently and its source is deep and remote from the mucosa, standard endoscopy frequently fails to reveal an obvious lesion, and the episodic pattern of pain and haemorrhage reflects transient ductal obstruction by clot.
additionalDifferentials: Bleeding peptic ulcer or duodenal lesion
Ruptured visceral artery aneurysm into the gut
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography with angiographic phases to detect a pseudoaneurysm and pancreatic pathology
Visceral (coeliac and splenic) angiography, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic through embolisation
Side-viewing endoscopy to observe blood issuing from the ampulla
Serum amylase and lipase and assessment for underlying chronic pancreatitis
Full blood count, coagulation profile, and crossmatch
Abdominal ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging to characterise a pseudocyst or ductal disease
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability from a major pseudoaneurysm rupture
Recurrent obscure bleeding with negative upper endoscopy
Known pancreatic pseudocyst with new bleeding
reference.prognosis: Untreated rupture of a visceral artery pseudoaneurysm carries a substantial mortality, but timely angiographic embolisation controls most cases; the overall outlook is also shaped by the severity of the underlying pancreatic disease.
pitfalls: Failing to consider the diagnosis in obscure bleeding associated with chronic pancreatitis or a pseudocyst
Stopping the workup after a normal standard endoscopy
Overlooking a raised amylase as a clue
Delaying angiographic embolisation in a patient with a known pseudoaneurysm
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Resuscitate haemodynamically with fluids and blood products and correct any coagulopathy
Control bleeding definitively with transarterial angiographic embolisation of the culprit splenic-artery pseudoaneurysm as first-line therapy
Proceed to surgery, such as arterial ligation or distal pancreatectomy, when embolisation fails, is not feasible, or bleeding recurs
Treat the underlying pancreatic disease, draining or resecting an associated pseudocyst and managing chronic pancreatitis
Monitor haemodynamic status and haemoglobin, and reassess for rebleeding with repeat imaging
Manage jointly with interventional radiology and hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgery
